fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. Verse 1 says the outcry is "…against their fellow Jews." The people crying out are pointing at their fellow Jews, and that's a hard thing to cry out about. Nehemiah, the governor of Judah, is about to hear every bit of it.
No army marches into this passage, baker. Verse 1 says the outcry is against their fellow Jews. That's the twist. The people crying out are pointing at their fellow Jews, not at the Samaritan army.

True, baker. Verse 3 says they are mortgaging their fields, vineyards and homes "…to get grain during the famine." Verse 2 says they need grain to eat and stay alive. Hungry families and a lot of pressure.

Right on, baker. Some of the people say in verse 5 that they are powerless to redeem their daughters "…because our fields and vineyards belong to others." The land is no longer theirs, and they can't redeem their daughters. I think that's a painful spot for any parent to stand in.
Not quite, baker. Nehemiah, the governor of Judah, says in verse 6, "…I became extremely angry…" He doesn't shrug off the outcry and the complaints. A calm, quiet Nehemiah isn't what the text shows.

That's right, baker. Nehemiah, the governor of Judah, says in verse 6, "When I heard their outcry and these complaints, I became extremely angry…" He doesn't stay calm and quiet. Then, after serious thought, he rebukes the nobles and officials.
You got it, baker. Nehemiah says, "You are exacting usury from your own brothers!" (Nehemiah 5:7). Usury is charging extra on what people borrow. And he says it about their own brothers.

Grain is a big deal in this passage, baker, but it's not the answer to this question. Nehemiah asks, "Shouldn’t you walk in the fear of our God to avoid the reproach of our foreign enemies?" (Nehemiah 5:9). The famine is already there. This question is about reproach from their foreign enemies.

That's the word, baker. Nehemiah says, "Please restore to them immediately their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses…" (Nehemiah 5:11). No "let me get back to you." He wants it all restored immediately.

Not so, baker. In verse 12 the nobles and officials reply, "We will restore it…" and say they "will require nothing more from them." They don't ask for time to think it over. They say they will do as Nehemiah says.

You've got it, baker. The nobles and officials reply, "We will restore it…" and say they "will require nothing more from them. We will do as you say." (Nehemiah 5:12). Their reply is a yes, and it says nothing about needing time.

Right, baker. Nehemiah tells it this way in verse 12: "So I summoned the priests and required of the nobles and officials an oath that they would do what they had promised." The priests are the ones he summons. The oath is required of the nobles and officials.

The scribes are a good guess, friend, but they aren't in this verse. Verse 12 says Nehemiah summoned "the priests" and required an oath of the nobles and officials. So the priests are the ones he summons.

Elders are not named in this verse, baker. Nehemiah says in verse 12, "So I summoned the priests and required of the nobles and officials an oath…" So the priests are the ones he summons for the oath.

The text doesn't say anyone backed out, friend. Verse 13 says the whole assembly said Amen and praised the LORD. Then it ends, "And the people did as they had promised." They followed through. I'll take a happy ending when the Bible gives me one.
No second round of arguing here, baker. Verse 13 says the whole assembly said Amen and praised the LORD. Then it says "…the people did as they had promised."

That's the number, baker. Nehemiah says in verse 14, "…from his twentieth year until his thirty-second year (twelve years total)…" That's the time he serves as governor, from the year King Artaxerxes appointed him. Twelve years is a long stretch.

Yes, baker. Nehemiah tells us in verse 14, "…neither I nor my brothers ate the food allotted to the governor." That food was allotted to the governor, and he and his brothers didn't eat it for those twelve years. The text goes on to say why in verse 15.

The priests have a part in this chapter, friend, but not here. Nehemiah says in verse 14, "…neither I nor my brothers ate the food allotted to the governor." That's the food he and his brothers didn't eat. The text doesn't mention food set aside for priests.

The text never mentions food from the palace, baker. Nehemiah says in verse 14, "…neither I nor my brothers ate the food allotted to the governor." That's the food named in the verse. Nothing there is said about the king's palace.
Not at all, baker. Nehemiah says in verse 16, "we did not acquire any land." He devoted himself to the construction of the wall. That's where his time went.

Right, baker. Nehemiah says in verse 16, "I devoted myself to the construction of the wall, and all my servants were gathered there for the work; we did not acquire any land." His time went to the wall, and no land was acquired. So the answer is False.

True, baker. Nehemiah tells us in verse 17, "There were 150 Jews and officials at my table, besides the guests from the surrounding nations." That's a full house. I've had six cutters at my counter and I thought THAT was crowded.

That's not the reason given, baker. Nehemiah says in verse 18 that he did not demand the food allotted to the governor "…because the burden on the people was so heavy." That's the reason the text gives. It doesn't say anything about the nobles paying.

The wall matters in this chapter, baker, but it's not in the prayer. Nehemiah prays in verse 19, "Remember me favorably, O my God, for all that I have done for this people." So he's asking God to remember him favorably for what he has done for the people.
